subject: health
unitTitle: Health Literacy and Decision Making in High School
title: Correction and reflection: reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame
focus: reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame
essentialQuestion: How do I turn health information I trust into a decision I can actually defend?
materials: two contrasting written health sources supplied by the course or guardian
keyPoints: Reviewing a decision means comparing the outcome with the information available at the time, identifying what changed, and revising the process without turning hindsight into self-blame.
A durable plan names the goal, constraints, feasible options, support and backup routes, plus the evidence or condition that should trigger review and revision.

For reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame, a strong response distinguishes fact from assumption, uses a fictional or public case, and includes a safe next step or appropriate source of support.
privacySafeScenario: Work a fictional high-school health decision end to end: name the influences, evaluate two competing sources, run the decision process, and state what evidence would change the decision. The learner never has to use a real decision from their own life.
studentTask: Build a decision organizer for a fictional person working on reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame. Record the goal, two influences or constraints, two options, the safest feasible choice, a support or backup route, and the evidence that would trigger a later revision.
knowledgeCheck: In two or three sentences, explain the most important distinction in reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame; use one lesson fact and name the evidence, safety check, or support route that makes the explanation dependable.
completionCriteria: The response completes every named part of the reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame task using the supplied fictional or public case.
The response uses at least two accurate details from the lesson instruction and distinguishes evidence from assumption.
The response gives a safe, feasible next step or support route and does not depend on private disclosure, body comparison, or recorded media proof.
adaptationChoices: The decision process may be written, typed, spoken to an adult, diagrammed, recorded on a graphic organizer, or built from sentence stems. A learner may substitute any scenario for another supplied scenario without penalty.
extensionChallenge: Apply reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame under a new constraint, compare two approaches, or explain the idea to someone else with an original fictional example, without completing another learner's graded work.
accessibilitySupports: Provide readable text plus optional audio or read-aloud support; no voice feature is required.
Chunk directions into one action at a time and show a worked example or model.
Allow typed, handwritten, spoken, drawn, manipulatives-based, or demonstrated responses when the standard permits.
Offer reduced-copying, extended-time, hidden-timer, movement-break, and low-distraction options.
Use captions, alt text, high-contrast print, keyboard access, and text-only fallbacks for media.
Preserve the learning target while adjusting quantity, pacing, representation, or response mode.

trustedAdultNote: This course teaches health information and does not diagnose; direct urgent safety or health concerns to a trusted adult or qualified professional.

optionalReflection.prompt: Invite the learner to notice one safe, optional example of reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame in daily life. No purchase, account creation, photograph, recording, or private disclosure is required.

neverRequires: This task never requires body weight, height, BMI, or body-fat percentage.
This task never requires calorie counting or a diet or weight-loss goal.
This task never requires disclosing private medical history, a diagnosis, or sexual history.
This task never requires a photograph, video, or voice recording of the learner as proof.
This task never requires a public performance or an audience.

contentProvenance.objective: Explain reviewing a decision after the fact without self-blame accurately using current, reliable health information rather than assumption or anecdote.
